name: Battle of Midway
info: Two United States carrier groups sank all four Japanese fleet carriers present near Midway Atoll in June 1942, six months after Pearl Harbor, and wrecked Admiral Yamamoto's plan to capture the atoll and destroy the American carriers.

facts.date: 4–7 June 1942; the Japanese Aleutian operation began a day earlier, on 3 June
facts.place: The sea near Midway Atoll, about 1,300 miles (2,100 km) north-west of Oahu in the Hawaiian chain, in the North Pacific
facts.sides: The United States Pacific Fleet under Admiral Chester Nimitz, with carrier groups under Frank Jack Fletcher and Raymond Spruance and 122 aircraft on Midway; the Japanese Combined Fleet under Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, with the carrier strike force (Kidō Butai) under Chūichi Nagumo, which sailed with 248 aircraft on four carriers
facts.outcome: The Japanese lost the carriers Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū and Hiryū and the heavy cruiser Mikuma, and 3,057 men; the United States lost the carrier Yorktown, the destroyer Hammann and 307 men. Japan did not take Midway.

t: American code breakers had partly read the Japanese naval code and knew the target and the likely date, while the Japanese remained largely unaware of their opponent's strength and positions even after the battle began.

All four Japanese fleet carriers present were sunk, three of them within minutes of the dive-bomber attacks that began at 10:22 on 4 June, while the American torpedo squadrons lost most of their aircraft without scoring a hit.
Japan lost about 3,000 men and many well-trained pilots, and its ability to replace losses in materiel and men became insufficient as American industrial and training capacity grew.
dyk: Yorktown, damaged at the Coral Sea a month before and expected to need months of repair, was made battle-ready at Pearl Harbor in 72 hours, with repair crews still aboard when she sailed.
ev: Yamamoto's plan to take Midway and destroy the American carriers is adopted after the Doolittle Raid on Tokyo
American code breakers confirm that the Japanese objective "AF" is Midway and give the attack date as 4 or 5 June
Midway-based aircraft find the Japanese occupation force, and the Japanese attack on the Aleutians begins
Nagumo's aircraft bomb Midway at about 06:34, and American torpedo squadrons attack the carriers without success
American dive bombers set Kaga, Sōryū and Akagi ablaze from 10:22
Hiryū's two strikes cripple Yorktown, and in the afternoon American bombers leave Hiryū burning
Yamamoto orders a general withdrawal to the west
Mikuma is sunk and Yorktown capsizes after submarine torpedoes

sections.background:
Japan's early offensives took British Hong Kong, the Philippines, British Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies, whose oil was particularly important to it, and planning for a second phase began as early as January 1942. Disagreements between the Imperial Army and the Imperial Navy, and between the Navy's Imperial General Headquarters and Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto's Combined Fleet, delayed a follow-up strategy until April 1942. Yamamoto won with a thinly veiled threat to resign. His main goal was to eliminate the American carrier forces, which he regarded as the principal threat to the Pacific campaign. The Doolittle Raid of 18 April 1942, in which 16 B-25 bombers launched from USS Hornet bombed Tokyo and other cities, was militarily insignificant but shocked the Japanese and showed a gap in the defences of the home islands.

Yamamoto reasoned that another attack on Pearl Harbor would draw out the whole American fleet, carriers included, but judged a direct attack too risky given the increased strength of American land-based air power on Hawaii. He chose Midway, a small atoll at the north-western end of the Hawaiian chain, about 1,300 miles (2,100 km) from Oahu. It was not especially important to Japan's wider intentions, but the Japanese expected the Americans to treat it as a vital outpost of Pearl Harbor and defend it vigorously. To win the Army's support, the Navy agreed to back an invasion of the Aleutian Islands of Attu and Kiska in the Alaska Territory. A one-day delay in Nagumo's sailing meant that Operation AL began on 3 June, a day before the Midway attack.
sections.forces:
Yamamoto's plan, Operation MI, required the coordination of several battle groups over hundreds of miles of sea. It rested on optimistic intelligence that only the carriers Enterprise and Hornet were available to the Pacific Fleet, and on a gross misjudgement of American morale. Yamamoto dispersed his forces, so that his battleships trailing the carriers by several hundred miles could not support them. Vice Admiral Nagumo's strike force had four carriers, Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū and Hiryū, with 248 aircraft, since Shōkaku was under repair and Zuikaku had lost almost half her air group at the Coral Sea. Beyond twelve destroyers it had two fast battleships, two heavy cruisers and one light cruiser. The carriers were vulnerable to fire, the combat air patrol had too few fighters, and there was no radar.

Admiral Chester Nimitz held Enterprise and Hornet under Rear Admiral Raymond Spruance, who replaced Vice Admiral William Halsey, ill with shingles, and recalled Rear Admiral Frank Jack Fletcher with Yorktown. Midway held 122 aircraft of the Navy, Marine Corps and Army Air Forces. Nimitz also had a critical advantage: U.S. cryptanalysts had partially broken the Japanese code JN-25b. They confirmed that the objective "AF" was Midway, partly through a ruse, a false uncoded report of a water shortage there, and gave him the date as 4 or 5 June and a complete Japanese order of battle.
sections.course:
On 3 June a PBY sighted the Japanese occupation force, and B-17s from Midway attacked it without hitting any ship. At 04:30 on 4 June Nagumo launched 36 D3A dive bombers and 36 B5N bombers with 36 Zero fighters against Midway. Radar picked them up at 05:53 and Marine fighters that intercepted them suffered heavy losses. The Japanese bombed Midway from 06:34 but did not neutralise it. Nagumo kept half his aircraft in reserve and at 07:15 ordered them re-armed for land targets. A scout then reported American ships at 07:40, and he reversed the order. At 08:20 came confirmation that a carrier was among them.

American carrier aircraft went in piecemeal from about 07:00. Torpedo Squadron 8 attacked at 09:20 and all 15 aircraft were shot down; Ensign George Gay was the only survivor of its 30 aircrew. Torpedo Squadron 6 lost 9 of 14, and 10 of 12 from Yorktown were shot down, with no hits. They drew the Zeros low, however, and at 10:22 dive bombers from Enterprise and Yorktown arrived undisturbed. Kaga took three to five hits, Akagi one bomb that exploded among armed and fuelled aircraft, and Sōryū at least three. Hiryū then hit Yorktown with three bombs and two torpedoes. Late in the afternoon American bombers hit Hiryū with four bombs, possibly five.
sections.aftermath:
Spruance, fearing a night encounter with Japanese surface forces, withdrew east after dark and turned west again at midnight. Yamamoto ordered a general withdrawal to the west. On 5 June the cruisers Mogami and Mikuma collided while avoiding the submarine Tambor, and Mikuma was sunk by Dauntlesses over the next two days. On 6 June the Japanese submarine I-168 torpedoed Yorktown, under tow, and the destroyer Hammann, which broke in two and sank with the loss of 80 lives. Yorktown capsized and sank at 07:01 on 7 June.

3,057 Japanese had died by the end of the battle: 2,181 aboard the four carriers (Akagi 267, Kaga 811, Hiryū 392, Sōryū 711) and 792 on the cruisers Mikuma and Mogami. Three hundred seven Americans were killed. Three American aviators were captured. Ensign Wesley Osmus was murdered aboard the destroyer Arashi, apparently on the captain's order, and Ensign Frank O'Flaherty and Bruno Gaido were interrogated and thrown overboard tied to water-filled kerosene cans. Japanese sailors rescued by American ships were interrogated, and one at least cooperated.

The Japanese public was told of a great victory. Only the Emperor and the highest naval staff knew the carrier and personnel losses. The wounded were isolated as "secret patients", and none of the flag officers was penalised.
sections.sources:
The original Japanese plans for the Midway attack are missing, so that Yamamoto's intentions for his battleships are inferred. One school of thought holds that they were to destroy whatever American ships came out in a daylight gun battle; another that he had no intention of using them. Many earlier accounts took the Aleutian operation for a feint, but the original Japanese plan had it begin at the same time as the Midway attack. Nagumo's detailed battle report of 15 June was closely guarded through the war.

The course of the day is told partly by those who were there. Lieutenant Clarence Dickinson recalled the attack on Kaga, Mitsuo Fuchida, who had led the attack on Pearl Harbor, described the hit on Akagi, and Nagumo's chief of staff Ryūnosuke Kusaka recorded its fires. Nimitz judged that Air Group Commander C. Wade McClusky's choice to persist in the search "decided the fate of our carrier task force and our forces at Midway". Later evidence suggests Nagumo did not receive the sighting report until 08:00, not 07:40. Samuel Morison noted in 1949 that Spruance was criticised for not pursuing the retreating Japanese, and Clay Blair argued in 1975 that he could not have launched aircraft after dark. Parshall and Tully dispute the view that the loss of veteran aircrew crippled the Japanese. Ballard found Yorktown in 1998; Petrel found Kaga and Akagi in October 2019.
sections.legacy:
The battle has often been called the turning point of the Pacific. John Keegan called it "the most stunning and decisive blow in the history of naval warfare", and Craig Symonds ranked it alongside Salamis, Trafalgar and Tsushima Strait. It allowed the Allies to take the strategic initiative before the first of the new Essex-class carriers appeared at the end of 1942, paving the way for the landings on Guadalcanal. Japan built three carriers in the time the U.S. Navy commissioned more than two dozen fleet and light carriers. Japan's replacement pilots had abbreviated training, while the United States rotated its veterans into training and command posts.

The Japanese rearmed and refuelled aircraft on the flight deck, drained unused fuel lines and fitted new carriers with two elevators and firefighting equipment. Midway showed the worth of pre-war cryptanalysis, which later made possible the shooting down of Yamamoto's aircraft in 1943.

Chicago Municipal Airport was renamed Midway in 1949, and Henderson Field on Guadalcanal was named for Major Lofton Henderson, killed in the battle. Midway Atoll was designated the Battle of Midway National Memorial in 2000. John Ford's 18-minute film The Battle of Midway won the 1942 Academy Award for Best Documentary.

summary: On 4 to 7 June 1942 American carrier aircraft sank four Japanese fleet carriers near Midway Atoll, after code breakers had given Admiral Nimitz the date and place of the attack. Japan lost 3,057 men and many pilots, and the United States Navy took the initiative in the Pacific.
references: Peter C. Smith, Midway Dauntless Victory; Fresh perspectives on America's Seminal Naval Victory of 1942 (Pen & Sword Maritime, 2007)
Alvin Kernan, The Unknown Battle of Midway (Yale University Press, 2005)
Edwin T. Layton, And I Was There: Pearl Harbor and Midway (W. Morrow, 1985)
Mitsuo Fuchida, Midway: The Battle that Doomed Japan, the Japanese Navy's Story (Naval Institute Press, 1955)
Douglas V. Smith, Carrier Battles: Command Decision in Harm's Way (Naval Institute Press, 2006)
notes: Article has no sources section: the sources section is built from the article's remarks on missing plans, the guarded report, eyewitness quotations, historians' views and the wreck discoveries.
Nagumo's launch time for reserve re-arming: article gives 07:15 order, scout sighting 07:40, 'later evidence suggests' 08:00 receipt.

Left out: the article's long 'Japanese shortcomings' speculation on Yamamoto's reading of the Aleutians attack (garbled and argumentative), and the 'Had Nagumo instead launched...' counterfactuals, the 'Impact' counterfactual on a Japanese victory, and the Japan-Germany Indian subcontinent claim (unsourced).
The article's Aftermath says the Japanese public was told of a victory and only the Emperor and top naval staff knew the losses; kept as written.
